name: LimitRange: defaults & bounds
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration and Security. Drill EVERY corner of namespace resource governance harder than the exam: compute ResourceQuota, object-count quota, scoped quota (BestEffort), LimitRange defaults, LimitRange min/max bounds, ratio limits, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix of a pod rejected by a quota. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: LimitRange — default requests & limits
questions.teach:
A **LimitRange** (type `Container`) injects resources into pods that omit them: `defaultRequest` supplies the **requests**, `default` supplies the **limits**. This is what lets a bare pod satisfy a compute quota. **Gotcha:** defaults are injected at admission — verify on the pod (`kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'`), never from your YAML.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-quotas`, create a LimitRange `defaults` (type `Container`) with `defaultRequest` cpu `200m` / memory `128Mi` and `default` (limits) cpu `500m` / memory `256Mi`. Then create pod `nodefaults` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container name `app`) with **no** resources block.

Target: pod `nodefaults`'s container ends up with requests cpu `200m` / memory `128Mi` and limits cpu `500m` / memory `256Mi`.
questions.hint: Apply the LimitRange (type Container, default + defaultRequest) FIRST, then `kubectl -n ckad-quotas run nodefaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`; check with jsonpath on `.spec.containers[0].resources`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: { name: defaults, namespace: ckad-quotas }
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    defaultRequest: { cpu: 200m, memory: 128Mi }
    default: { cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi }
YAML
kubectl -n ckad-quotas run nodefaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600

verification.description: nodefaults inherited requests 200m/128Mi + limits 500m/256Mi from the LimitRange

questions.eli5:
Picture a daycare where every kid (pod) needs a lunchbox before they're allowed in. A **LimitRange** is the kind helper at the door who, if a kid shows up with **no lunchbox**, hands them a standard one automatically — so nobody gets turned away for forgetting.

A LimitRange of type `Container` fills in two things when a container leaves them blank:

- **defaultRequest** → becomes the container's **requests** (what it reserves): cpu `200m`, memory `128Mi`.
- **default** → becomes the container's **limits** (its ceiling): cpu `500m`, memory `256Mi`.

That's the magic that lets a bare `kubectl run` pod survive in a namespace that has a compute quota: the quota demands requests *and* limits, and the LimitRange quietly supplies them at the door.

Here you apply the LimitRange first, then launch pod `nodefaults` with **no** resources block — and it still ends up with the four values above baked in.

**Watch out for:**

- The defaults are stamped on at **admission time**, not written in your YAML. So you must verify on the *created pod*: `kubectl get pod nodefaults -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'` — looking at your original YAML tells you nothing.
- **Apply the LimitRange BEFORE creating the pod.** A LimitRange only affects pods created *after* it exists; it never retro-fixes existing pods.
- `default` means *limits*, `defaultRequest` means *requests* — the naming is easy to flip. Get them backwards and your values land in the wrong place.
- If a container *does* set its own values, the LimitRange leaves them alone — defaults only fill gaps.
questions.deepDive:
## LimitRange defaults — full rundown

### Mental model
A **LimitRange** is a namespace-scoped admission mutator/validator for per-object resource values. The `Container` type with `default`/`defaultRequest` **injects** resources into containers that omit them. This is the bridge that lets bare pods satisfy a compute ResourceQuota.

### The two default knobs
| Field | Injected into | If the container already sets it |
|---|---|---|
| `defaultRequest` | `resources.requests` | left untouched |
| `default` | `resources.limits` | left untouched |

> Mnemonic: **default = limits**, **defaultRequest = requests**.

### Create it, then a bare pod
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    defaultRequest: { cpu: 200m, memory: 128Mi }
    default:        { cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi }
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f defaults.yaml          # MUST exist before the pod
kubectl -n ckad-quotas run nodefaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get pod nodefaults \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'
# {"limits":{"cpu":"500m","memory":"256Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"128Mi"}}
```

### Injection interaction rules
| Container declares | Result after LimitRange |
|---|---|
| nothing | gets both defaultRequest → requests and default → limits |
| only `limits` | requests default to the **limits** values (not defaultRequest!) |
| only `requests` | limits default to `default` (if request ≤ default) |
| both | unchanged |

> Subtle: if you set only `limits`, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request *before* the LimitRange default would apply — a classic trap.

### LimitRange types
| `type` | Governs |
|---|---|
| `Container` | per-container requests/limits (this lesson) |
| `Pod` | sum across all containers in a pod (min/max only; no defaults) |
| `PersistentVolumeClaim` | min/max storage requests |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Order matters**: a LimitRange only mutates pods created *after* it. Apply it first; it never patches existing pods.
- **Verify on the live pod**, not your source YAML — defaults appear only post-admission.
- `default` is **limits**; `defaultRequest` is **requests**. Swapping them is the #1 mistake.
- Only `type: Container` (and `Pod`/`PVC`) are valid — a typo in `type` silently does nothing useful.
- Defaults never override explicit values; they only fill omissions.
- One namespace can hold multiple LimitRanges; their constraints combine.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl apply -f defaults.yaml   # type: Container, default + defaultRequest
kubectl -n ckad-quotas run nodefaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get pod nodefaults -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
```

questions.title: LimitRange — min and max bounds
questions.teach:
A LimitRange (type `Container`) also enforces **per-container bounds**: `min` is the floor and `max` the ceiling. A container requesting below `min` or limiting above `max` is rejected at admission.

**Gotcha:** a bare integer `cpu: 1` in YAML is read as a number — quote it (`cpu: "1"`) so it round-trips as the string `1`.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-quotas`, create a LimitRange `constraints` (type `Container`) with `min` cpu `100m` / memory `64Mi` and `max` cpu `1` / memory `1Gi`.

Target: `constraints` has min cpu `100m`, min memory `64Mi`, max cpu `1`, max memory `1Gi`.
questions.hint: Apply a LimitRange YAML with `type: Container`, `min: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}`, `max: {cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi}`.

verification.description: constraints LimitRange: min cpu 100m/mem 64Mi, max cpu 1/mem 1Gi

questions.eli5:
The same door-helper (LimitRange) can also be a **bouncer with a height chart**: "you must be *at least this tall* to ride, and *no taller than this* to fit." For containers, that's a floor and a ceiling on how much CPU and memory a single container may ask for.

This LimitRange of type `Container` sets:

- **min** — the floor: cpu `100m`, memory `64Mi`. A container asking for *less* is refused.
- **max** — the ceiling: cpu `1`, memory `1Gi`. A container asking for *more* is refused.

So any container in this namespace must live in the band 100m–1 core of CPU and 64Mi–1Gi of memory, or admission rejects it.

**Watch out for:**

- A bare integer like `cpu: 1` in YAML is parsed as a **number**, but Kubernetes stores CPU as a **quantity string**. Write it quoted — `cpu: "1"` — so it round-trips as the string `"1"` the grader expects (memory values like `1Gi` carry a unit, so they're already strings).
- `min`/`max` bound **each container individually**, not the pod total — that's what the `Pod` type is for.
- These bounds are about what a container *requests/limits*, enforced at admission. A violating pod is rejected with a message naming the offending resource and bound.
- min and max are independent of the `default`/`defaultRequest` from the previous step; you can combine all of them in one LimitRange.
- Don't confuse this with ResourceQuota: a quota caps the **namespace total**; a LimitRange min/max caps **a single container**.
questions.deepDive:
## LimitRange min/max bounds — full rundown

### Mental model
A `Container`-type LimitRange can enforce a **floor (`min`)** and **ceiling (`max`)** on each container's resource requests/limits. These are validated at admission; a violating pod is rejected. Bounds are **per-container**, not per-pod.

### Create it
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: constraints
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    min: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }
    max: { cpu: "1",  memory: 1Gi }
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f constraints.yaml
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get limitrange constraints -o yaml
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe limitrange constraints
```

### All the Container-type fields
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `min` | lowest request/limit a container may set |
| `max` | highest request/limit a container may set |
| `default` | injected **limit** when omitted |
| `defaultRequest` | injected **request** when omitted |
| `maxLimitRequestRatio` | cap on `limit ÷ request` |

> One `limits[]` entry can carry min, max, defaults, and ratio together.

### How a value is judged
For each resource, after any defaults are applied:
```
min ≤ request      and      limit ≤ max
```
A request below `min` or a limit above `max` → rejected:
```
maximum cpu usage per Container is 1, but limit is 2
minimum memory usage per Container is 64Mi, but request is 32Mi
```

### The YAML-quoting trap
Kubernetes stores resource quantities as **strings**. A bare integer gets re-serialised and may not round-trip as the literal you typed:
| You wrote | Stored as | Safe? |
|---|---|---|
| `cpu: "1"` | `"1"` | ✅ exact |
| `cpu: 1` | `"1"` *(usually, but relies on quantity normalisation)* | ⚠️ quote it |
| `memory: 1Gi` | `"1Gi"` | ✅ (unit forces string) |
Always **quote bare-integer CPU** (`"1"`, `"2"`) on the exam.

### min/max vs ResourceQuota
| | Scope | What it limits |
|---|---|---|
| LimitRange min/max | per **container** | an individual container's request/limit |
| ResourceQuota | per **namespace** | the *sum* across all pods |

Both can coexist; a pod must satisfy both.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- Bounds are **per-container** — use `type: Pod` for pod-wide sums.
- **Quote bare integers** for CPU so the stored value matches exactly.
- With a compute quota present, `min`/`max` combine with the quota's totals — a container can be individually legal yet still blow the namespace sum.
- If both a default and a min/max exist, the default must itself fall within min/max or admission fails.
- `min`/`max` apply to *both* requests and limits as appropriate (request ≥ min, limit ≤ max).

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    min: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }
    max: { cpu: "1",  memory: 1Gi }
```
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe limitrange constraints
```

questions.title: LimitRange — maxLimitRequestRatio
questions.teach:
`maxLimitRequestRatio` on a LimitRange caps how far a container's **limit** may exceed its **request** per resource. `cpu: 4` means `limit/request` must be ≤ 4 — a container requesting `100m` can't limit above `400m`.

**Gotcha:** the ratio constrains the gap, not absolute values — it's independent of `min`/`max`, and a pod violating it is rejected at admission.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-quotas`, create a LimitRange `ratios` (type `Container`) with `maxLimitRequestRatio` cpu `4`.

Target: `ratios` has `spec.limits[0].maxLimitRequestRatio.cpu` = `4`.
questions.hint: Apply a LimitRange YAML: `type: Container`, `maxLimitRequestRatio: {cpu: "4"}` (quote it so it round-trips as a string).
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: { name: ratios, namespace: ckad-quotas }
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    maxLimitRequestRatio: { cpu: "4" }
YAML
questions.eli5:
Here's a different kind of rule for the same door-helper (LimitRange): it doesn't cap how big or small you can be — it caps **how greedy your spike can be compared to what you reserved.**

`maxLimitRequestRatio` says: your *limit* (the most you can spike to) can be at most N times your *request* (what you reserved). With `cpu: 4`, the limit must be **no more than 4×** the request. So a container reserving `100m` of CPU may spike to at most `400m`; reserve `250m` and you can spike to `1000m`. Ask for a wider gap and you're turned away.

Why would anyone want this? It stops a container from reserving a tiny sliver but then being *allowed* to balloon enormously — which makes the whole namespace behave predictably.

**Watch out for:**

- The ratio constrains the **gap** between limit and request, nothing else. It's **independent of min/max and of absolute values** — a container can be within min/max yet still violate the ratio, and vice versa.
- It's checked **per resource**: `maxLimitRequestRatio.cpu: 4` governs only CPU; memory is unconstrained unless you add `memory` too.
- Quote the number: `maxLimitRequestRatio: { cpu: "4" }`. A bare `4` may not round-trip as the string `"4"` the grader checks for.
- A pod that breaks the ratio is rejected at admission with a message like `cpu max limit to request ratio per Container is 4, but provided ratio is 5`.
- It only bites when a container sets **both** a request and a limit for that resource (there has to be a ratio to measure).
questions.deepDive:
## LimitRange maxLimitRequestRatio — full rundown

### Mental model
`maxLimitRequestRatio` caps the **burst factor** of a container: how many times larger its `limit` may be than its `request`, per resource. It constrains the *gap*, independent of absolute min/max. This discourages "reserve little, burst huge" containers that make namespace capacity unpredictable.

### The rule
For each resource with a ratio set:
```
limit / request ≤ maxLimitRequestRatio
```
With `cpu: 4`:
| request | max allowed limit |
|---|---|
| 100m | 400m |
| 250m | 1000m (1 core) |
| 500m | 2 |

### Create it
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: ratios
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    maxLimitRequestRatio: { cpu: "4" }
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f ratios.yaml
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get limitrange ratios \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.limits[0].maxLimitRequestRatio.cpu}{"\n"}'   # 4
```

### How it interacts with the other knobs
| Knob | Constrains | Independent of ratio? |
|---|---|---|
| `min`/`max` | absolute per-container value | yes |
| `default`/`defaultRequest` | fills omitted values | ratio checked *after* defaults applied |
| `maxLimitRequestRatio` | `limit ÷ request` | — |

A container can pass min/max and still fail the ratio, or vice versa — all applicable constraints must hold simultaneously.

### When it applies
- Only when a container sets **both** a request and a limit for that resource (otherwise there's no ratio to compute).
- Per-resource: setting `cpu` leaves `memory` unconstrained unless you also add `memory`.
- Combined form in one LimitRange entry:
  ```yaml
  spec:
    limits:
    - type: Container
      min: { cpu: 100m }
      max: { cpu: "2" }
      maxLimitRequestRatio: { cpu: "4" }
  ```

### Rejection message
```
cpu max limit to request ratio per Container is 4, but provided ratio is 5.000000
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Quote the number** (`cpu: "4"`) so it stores as the string the grader expects.
- The ratio is **per resource** — don't assume CPU's ratio covers memory.
- Independent of `min`/`max`: a value within bounds can still violate the ratio.
- Only evaluated when both request and limit are present (possibly after LimitRange defaults inject them).
- jsonpath to read it: `.spec.limits[0].maxLimitRequestRatio.cpu`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    maxLimitRequestRatio: { cpu: "4" }
```
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get limitrange ratios \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.limits[0].maxLimitRequestRatio.cpu}'
```
